summary: Seal Beach packs roughly 24,500 people into just under 12 square miles, yet almost half of that land area belongs to the Naval Weapons Station Seal Beach — one of the last active military installations on the Southern California coast — which means the actual residential footprint is remarkably compact and almost entirely flat, pressed between the Pacific and the wetlands of the San Gabriel River. That defense presence anchors a significant share of local employment alongside Boeing's nearby facilities in Huntington Beach and the broader aerospace-defense corridor stretching through Orange County, so this is partly a bedroom community for greater Long Beach and Irvine commuters but not entirely — switching employers in the defense sector doesn't necessarily require a zip-code change. The town's walkable Main Street runs a few short blocks to the pier, lined with independent restaurants, coffee shops, and small retail that give the commercial core a distinct identity rather than a generic strip-mall feel. Climate-wise, 74°F average highs and over nine hours of daily sunshine year-round make the coast usable in every season, and the pier and beach path offer genuine evening-walk infrastructure without needing a car. The affordability math, though, is revealing: a median home value around $492,000 against a median household income near $83,000 yields a price-to-income ratio of roughly 5.9×, and median rent at $2,419 consumes about 35% of that gross income — manageable but tight, especially given that the housing stock skews older and inventory is limited by the military reservation's footprint. Seal Beach is essentially a small coastal town whose geography is permanently constrained by a federal fence line, which simultaneously caps development pressure and ensures that housing supply will never meaningfully expand.
